# Introduction and Overview

In this assignment, structured web data acquisition and JSON data reshaping are applied to analyze scientific history via the Nobel Prize Developer Zone API [@nobelprizeAPI].

Using the Version 2.1 REST API, laureate-level records across the physical sciences (specifically Physics and Chemistry) are ingested. The raw data are parsed from hierarchical, nested JSON documents into rectangular, tidy data frames using the `jsonlite` [@jsonlite] and `tidyverse` [@tidyverse] ecosystems.

Beyond standard frequency counts, this study investigates historical mobility, collaboration, and career trajectories of famed scientists. Specifically, this work aims to examine scientific migration ("brain drain"), age distributions at time of recognition, institutional concentration of awards, seasonal birth distributions, and repeat prize winners.

# Approach

1.  Ingest API data

- Retrieve records from the `https://api.nobelprize.org/2.1/laureates` endpoint using `httr2`

- Parse raw JSON strings into structured R objects using `jsonlite::fromJSON`.

2.  Reshape and tidy nested structures

- Unnest nested array columns into tidy formats

3.  Investigate five research questions

- Which countries have experienced the largest net "brain drain" versus "brain gain" among Physics and Chemistry laureates?

- How has the average age of laureates at the time of their award changed over the decades in Physics compared to Chemistry?

- Which universities or research institutions have produced the most Nobel laureates across Physics and Chemistry?

- Does the distribution of birth months among Physics and Chemistry laureates show evidence of a "relative age effect"?

- Which individuals have won multiple Nobel prizes in Physics or Chemistry (or crossed between both), and what was the time gap between their awards?

4.  Summarize analysis with visualizations and tables

# Codebase

## Data loading

```{r}
#| label: library-load
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(httr2)
library(jsonlite)
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
```

```{r}
#| label: api-try-catch
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

get_nobel_data <- function(file = "laureates.rds") {

  if (file.exists(file)) {
    return(readRDS(file))
  }
  
  url <- "https://api.nobelprize.org/2.1/laureates?limit=1000"
  
  data <- tryCatch(
    {
      res <- fromJSON(url)
      df <- res$laureates
      saveRDS(df, file)
      df
    },
    error = function(e) {
      return(NULL)
    }
  )
  
  return(data)
}
```

```{r}
#| label: get-data
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

laureates_raw <- get_nobel_data()

nrow(laureates_raw)

ncol(laureates_raw)
```

## Data tidying and unnesting

In the Nobel Prize API, institutional affiliations are stored as nested list-columns. An individual award record may contain a single affiliated institution, multiple concurrent institutions, or none at all (represented as an empty or missing data frame).

Directly unnesting this column causes indexing errors and row-multiplication issues. To resolve this, `purrr::map_chr()` iterates row-by-row through the list-column using defensive validation logic.

This approach flattens the nested structures into consistent, vector-safe character strings while preserving the one-row-per-award observation granularity required for tidy analysis.

```{r}

laureates_clean <- laureates_raw |> 
  mutate(id = id,
         known_name = knownName$en,
         birth_date = birth$date,
         birth_country = birth$place$country$en,
         nobelPrizes = nobelPrizes,
         .keep = "none"
          ) |> 
  unnest(nobelPrizes) |> 
  mutate(
    id = id,
    known_name = known_name,
    birth_date = birth_date,
    birth_country = birth_country,
    award_year = as.numeric(awardYear),
    category = category$en,
    affiliations = affiliations,
    .keep = "none"
  ) |>
  filter(category %in% c("Physics", "Chemistry"))
  

```

Using date parsing and regex, birth dates are transformed into chronological `age_at_award`, award `decade`, and ordered `birth_month` factors while preserving missing records.

```{r}

laureates_tidy <- laureates_clean |> 
  mutate(
    affiliation_name = map_chr(affiliations, ~ {
      if (is.data.frame(.x) && "name" %in% names(.x) && nrow(.x) > 0) {
        return(.x$name$en[1])
      }
      return(NA_character_)
    }),
    affiliation_country = map_chr(affiliations, ~ {
      if (is.data.frame(.x) && "country" %in% names(.x) && nrow(.x) > 0) {
        return(.x$country$en[1])
      }
      return(NA_character_)
    }),
    birth_year = as.numeric(str_extract(birth_date, "^[0-9]{4}")),
    birth_month = factor(
      format(as.Date(birth_date), "%b"),
      levels = month.abb
    ),
    age_at_award = award_year - birth_year,
    decade = (award_year %/% 10) * 10
  )
```

## Question 1

### Which countries have experienced the largest net "brain drain" versus "brain gain" among Physics and Chemistry laureates?

```{r}
#| label: question-1
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

mobile_laureates <- laureates_tidy |>
  filter(!is.na(birth_country), !is.na(affiliation_country)) |>
  filter(birth_country != affiliation_country)

drain <- mobile_laureates |>
  count(country = birth_country, name = "emigrated")

gain <- mobile_laureates |>
  count(country = affiliation_country, name = "immigrated")

net_mobility <- full_join(gain, 
                          drain, 
                          by = "country") |>
  replace_na(list(immigrated = 0, 
                  emigrated = 0)) |>
  mutate(net_gain = immigrated - emigrated) |>
  arrange(desc(net_gain))

top_gainers <- head(net_mobility, 5) |> 
  mutate(Status = "Top Net Gainers")
top_losers  <- tail(net_mobility, 5) |> 
  arrange(net_gain) |> 
  mutate(Status = "Top Net Losers")
```

```{r}
#| label: question-1-summary
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

mobility_summary_table <- bind_rows(
  top_gainers, 
  top_losers) |>
  select(Status, 
         Country = country, 
         Immigrated = immigrated, 
         Emigrated = emigrated, 
         `Net Gain` = net_gain)

knitr::kable(mobility_summary_table, caption = "Net Mobility in Physics and Chemistry")
```

```{r}
#| label: question-1-plot
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

q1_plot_data <- net_mobility |>
  filter(abs(net_gain) >= 2) |>
  mutate(
    type = if_else(net_gain > 0, "Net Gain", "Net Loss"),
    country = fct_reorder(country, net_gain)
  )

q1_plot_data |>  ggplot(aes(x = net_gain, y = country, fill = type)) + 
  geom_col() + 
  labs(
    title = "Net Scientific Migration in Physics & Chemistry",
    caption = "data sourced from Nobel Prize API",
    x = "Net Laureate Balance (Immigrated - Emigrated)",
    y = NULL,
    fill = NULL
  ) + 
  theme_standard() +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )
```

The analysis reveals an asymmetric geographic concentration of scientific talent in Physics and Chemistry. The United States is by far the largest net beneficiary of international scientific talent mobility. Historial nations such as Prussia and Austria-Hungary experienced the greatest net depletion of scientific talent, with contemporaries of Russia and China also demonstrating net losses.

## Question 2

### How has the average age of laureates at the time of their award changed over the decades in Physics compared to Chemistry?

```{r}
#| label: question-2
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

age_trends <- laureates_tidy |>
  filter(!is.na(age_at_award), 
         !is.na(decade)) |>
  group_by(decade, 
           category) |>
  summarize(
    laureates = n(),
    mean_age = round(mean(age_at_award), 1),
    median_age = round(median(age_at_award), 1),
    min_age = min(age_at_award),
    max_age = max(age_at_award),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: question-2-summary
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

age_summary_table <- age_trends |>
  select(decade, 
         category, 
         mean_age) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = category, 
              values_from = mean_age) |>
  mutate(difference_chem_minus_phys = round(Chemistry - Physics, 1))

knitr::kable(
  age_summary_table, 
  col.names = c("Decade", "Chemistry Mean Age", "Physics Mean Age", "Difference (Chem - Phys)"),
  caption = "Decadal Mean Laureate Age at Award: Chemistry vs. Physics"
)
```

```{r}

annual_ages <- laureates_tidy |>
  filter(!is.na(age_at_award)) |>
  group_by(award_year, 
           category) |>
  summarize(mean_age = mean(age_at_award), 
            .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = category, 
              values_from = mean_age)

crossover_year <- annual_ages |>
  filter(award_year >= 1990, Physics > Chemistry) |>
  slice(1) |>
  pull(award_year)

crossover_year
```

Gemini was used to assist in adding shaded back panel to plot.

```{r}
#| label: question-2-plot
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

age_trends |> ggplot(aes(x = decade, 
                         y = mean_age, 
                         color = category, 
                         group = category)) + 
  annotate(
    "rect",
    xmin = -Inf,
    xmax = crossover_year,
    ymin = -Inf,
    ymax = Inf,
    fill = "gray90",
    alpha = 0.5
  ) +
  
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = crossover_year, 
    linetype = "dotted", 
    color = "gray40", 
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = crossover_year - 2,
    y = 48,
    label = paste0("Pre-", crossover_year, ":\nChem older than Phys"),
    hjust = 1,
    size = 3.2,
    color = "gray30",
    fontface = "italic"
  ) +
  
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", 
              se = FALSE, 
              linetype = "dashed", 
              alpha = 0.5) +
  
  labs(
    title = "Average Age of Nobel Laureates at Time of Award (by Decade)",
    caption = "data sourced from Nobel Prize API",
    x = "Award Year (by decade)",
    y = "Average Age at Award",
    color = "Discipline"
  ) +
  
  theme_standard() + 
  
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )

```

Prior to 1991, Chemistry laureates were consistently older than physicists. After 1991, modern Physics overtook Chemistry in average recipient age.

## Question 3

### Which universities or research institutions have produced the most Nobel laureates across Physics and Chemistry?

```{r}
#| label: question-3
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

institution_counts <- laureates_tidy |>
  filter(!is.na(affiliation_name)) |>
  count(affiliation_name, 
        category, 
        name = "awards")

top_institutions_overall <- institution_counts |>
  group_by(affiliation_name) |>
  summarize(total_awards = sum(awards), 
            .groups = "drop") |>
  slice_max(total_awards, 
            n = 10, 
            with_ties = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: question-3-summary
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

top_10_table <- institution_counts |>
  semi_join(top_institutions_overall, 
            by = "affiliation_name") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = category, 
              values_from = awards, 
              values_fill = 0) |>
  mutate(Total = Chemistry + Physics) |>
  arrange(desc(Total))

knitr::kable(
  top_10_table,
  col.names = c("Institution", "Chemistry", "Physics", "Total Awards"),
  caption = "Top 10 Research Institutions by Nobel Laureates in Physical Sciences"
)
```

```{r}
#| label: question-3-plot
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

q3_plot_data <- institution_counts |>
  semi_join(top_institutions_overall, 
            by = "affiliation_name") |>
  mutate(affiliation_name = fct_reorder(affiliation_name, 
                                        awards, 
                                        .fun = sum))

q3_plot_data |> ggplot(aes(x = awards, 
                           y = affiliation_name, 
                           fill = category)) +
  geom_col() +
  
  labs(
    title = "Top 10 Institutional Hubs: Physics & Chemistry",
    caption = "data sourced from Nobel Prize API",
    x = "Number of Laureates",
    y = NULL,
    fill = "Discipline"
  ) +
  theme_standard() +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )
```

To extend this work, a data set that tracks national population estimates over time could be leveraged to normalize some of these approaches.
